passage: Tariq ran out of his London school. "Mum! Abebe did the thing with the thing and Miss was cross!" Mum blinked. "Who's Abebe? What thing?" "The THING!" Tariq said, as if she had been there. passage: In the Kochi preschool, Aadhya pulled the doll out of Ishita's arms. Ishita burst into tears. The teacher sat down with both girls and a set of face cards. qa.a: A set of face cards.

qa.q: What did the teacher want Aadhya to understand by asking how she would feel?
qa.a: The teacher hoped Aadhya would feel what Ishita felt, sad and cross, by imagining it happening to herself.

passage: From our balcony in Bhopal I can see straight into the neighbours' front room. Last evening, five-year-old Wasim knocked down his baby sister's block tower and laughed. She wailed. His uncle, Pankaj, didn't shout. He fetched two sock puppets. One puppet built a tower; the other knocked it over. "Oh no," said the first puppet, in a small voice. "I worked so hard on that." Pankaj asked Wasim, "What is this puppet feeling?" Wasim was quiet for a moment, watching. "Sad." Then he picked up the blocks and started building again for his sister. I couldn't hear everything after that. But I saw him hand her the top block.

qa.q: What did Pankaj fetch after the tower fell?
qa.a: Two sock puppets.

qa.q: What did Pankaj seem to hope for when he asked what the puppet was feeling?
qa.a: Pankaj seemed calm and patient, hoping Wasim would notice his sister's sadness through the puppet rather than through a scolding.

qa.q: Why might pretend play work better than shouting here?
qa.a: Seeing it happen to a puppet lets Wasim step outside himself and feel how the tower-builder feels, without being defensive.

qa.q: How might Wasim's sister feel when he hands her the top block?
qa.a: She likely feels comforted and included, and her upset eases as her tower is rebuilt.

grounding: Shows, through a neighbour's account, a caregiver using pretend play to help a young child see how another feels.

passage:

passage: Farhan, you're angry your friend chose someone else for his team? Listen to your Akash Nana. When I was nine, in Jabalpur, my best friend Prakash wanted a kite for his birthday. I wanted to give him marbles, because I loved marbles. But then I thought, no, Prakash loves kites, not marbles. So I bought a kite. I was so proud of that thought! Then, one month later, Prakash picked a new boy, Salim, as his partner for the school sports. I was furious. I told everyone Prakash was a traitor. I couldn't think at all why he'd do it. Only later I learnt Salim was new and had no friends. Prakash was being kind. I had understood the kite. I couldn't understand the partner, because I was too hurt to think.

qa.q: What did Prakash want for his birthday?
qa.a: A kite.

qa.q: Why couldn't young Akash see why Prakash chose Salim?

qa.a: He could have asked Prakash why before calling him a traitor, which would have shown him Prakash was being kind to a new boy.

qa.a: Salim, new and without friends, likely felt relieved and welcomed when Prakash picked him.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a child beginning to see that a friend wants different things, but struggling when his own strong feelings take over.

passage: The picnic was cancelled because of the rain, and Anand and his sister Tanuja were stuck in the flat all Saturday with one TV. Anand wanted cricket highlights. Tanuja wanted her cartoon. "Fine," Anand said, surprising himself. "You watch first. You've been waiting all week for that episode." Tanuja stared at him. He felt quite grown-up. Then, at four, the match started live, and Tanuja asked for just ten more minutes. Anand's face went hot. "You always get your way!" he shouted, and snatched the remote. Tanuja cried. Anand stood there, remote in hand, knowing somewhere inside that she had only asked for ten minutes. He couldn't make himself give it back. Not yet.

qa.q: Why was the picnic cancelled?
qa.a: Because of the rain.

qa.q: Why could Anand see what Tanuja wanted in the morning but not at four?
qa.a: In the morning he felt calm and grown-up, so he could think about her wishes; when the live match started, his strong excitement and frustration swamped that understanding.

qa.q: What could Anand try next time his feelings get very strong?
qa.a: He could take a breath and remember what he did in the morning, or suggest a fair plan like taking turns every half hour.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel when Anand snatches the remote after being kind earlier?
qa.a: She probably feels hurt and confused, since he had just been so fair to her.

grounding: Shows an older child beginning to understand his sister wants different things, but losing that understanding when his own strong feelings take over.

passage: In the colony lane in Kochi, Gautam heard Thomas telling everyone the zoo trip was on Tuesday. Gautam knew it had moved to Thursday. passage: At the morning assembly in the Nagpur school, Deepak stood in the fourth row with a new haircut his uncle had given him the night before. It was too short at the back. Yogesh bhaiya,

Weird thing, though. At robotics club on Thursday, a class-twelve senior told me the same happened to him in class nine. He said it lasted a few months, then he found the robotics lot.

So maybe not nobody. Did it happen to you too? You never said.

Sahil

qa.a: Sahil could keep going to the robotics club and talk to people like the senior, who have been through something similar.

qa.a: He would likely feel touched that Sahil trusted him, and want to share his own story to show Sahil isn't alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling the experience is unique and everyone is watching, and the feeling starting to soften after meeting someone older.

passage: Jyoti, you asked for the most embarrassing thing that happened to Rafiq at fourteen, so here it is. Annual day, the school stage. I was playing a tree in the drama. A tree! passage: Salma, who taught English at the village school near Hassan, noticed Uday at the back again with his feet tucked under the bench. His shoes had split at the toes. passage: In their small São Paulo apartment, Priscila heard the bedroom door slam. Her daughter Nadia, sixteen, had got a bad mark in physics. "My life is over," Nadia shouted. "Everyone will know. You don't understand. Nobody has ever failed like this." Priscila felt the old urge to say, I failed physics twice, it's nothing. She held it back. She sat on the edge of the bed. "That sounds awful. Tell me." Nadia talked for twenty minutes. Priscila mostly nodded. The next week, at dinner, she mentioned casually that Nadia's cousin had once failed chemistry and now taught it. Nadia rolled her eyes. But a month later, she said, "Maybe people forget about marks faster than I thought."

qa.q: How long did Nadia talk after Priscila sat on the bed?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Priscila hold back from saying she had failed physics twice?
qa.a: Priscila felt the urge to comfort with her own story but was cautious, sensing it might feel dismissive while Nadia was upset.

qa.q: What approach helped widen Nadia's view, and why did it work?
qa.a: Listening first, then a week later casually mentioning a cousin's story, let Nadia hear it without feeling corrected.

qa.q: How might Nadia see her bad mark a month later?
qa.a: Nadia seems calmer, starting to see that others don't remember marks as much as she feared.

grounding: Shows a parent recognising a teenager's self-focus as normal, listening without dismissing, and widening the view over time.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the Jaipur school, the warden, Zainab, found Nirmala, fifteen, curled on her bed on a Sunday. "They're all talking about me," Nirmala said. "Because I cried in the dining hall. Nobody has ever been so homesick." Zainab had seen this almost every year. She didn't say so. She sat with her. "Being far from home is really hard. Tell me what you miss." Nirmala talked about her grandmother's garden. Zainab listened. The following Sunday, Zainab invited three girls to help her plant marigolds by the gate, Nirmala among them. While they dug, one girl said she had cried every night for a month in her first term. Nirmala stared. "You?" Zainab kept her eyes on the soil and smiled.

qa.q: What did Zainab invite the girls to plant?
qa.a: Marigolds by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Zainab not tell Nirmala that this happened almost every year?
qa.a: Zainab felt compassion and understood that pointing out how common it was might make Nirmala feel dismissed, so she listened first.

qa.q: How did the marigold planting widen Nirmala's view?
qa.a: It brought her together with other girls, one of whom shared her own homesickness, so Nirmala could learn she wasn't the only one.

qa.q: How might the girl who admitted crying every night feel after sharing?
qa.a: She might feel a bit exposed but also glad, seeing that her story helped Nirmala feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a hostel warden treating a teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listening kindly, and gently widening her view over time.

passage: Crack! Neelam's elbow knocked the clay cup off the shelf in Nani's village kitchen. A crack ran down its side. Neelam put it back quickly, crack facing the wall. Ritu mausi came in. "Neelam, did the cup fall?" "No." "There's a crack in it." "It was always like that," Neelam said, eyes on the floor. Ritu mausi knelt. "You're not in trouble, sweetheart. Cups break. qa.q: How might Ritu mausi feel when Neelam admits it?

passage: In the Madrid flat, orange juice dripped off the table onto the rug. Lucia stood beside the empty glass, hands behind her back. Rania, her babysitter, came in. "Oh! What happened?" passage: At the Hyderabad preschool, the class water jug lay on its side and a puddle spread across the floor. Manjula stood next to it, holding the tap. qa.q: How might Hansa Miss feel seeing the water on Manjula's shoes?

passage: Exam week, and the power in their Kanpur colony kept going off. Uma sat on the steps with Jyoti, holding a torch over her notes. "Is your papa home in the day now?" Jyoti asked. "My mummy said his factory closed." "Everything's fine," Uma said quickly. "He's just on leave." She didn't want to know more. When Mummy and Papa talked in low voices, she turned up the radio. When they looked at her, she said, "I'm fine." But she hadn't slept well all week, and today she'd shouted at her little brother for touching her pencil box. Jyoti didn't push. qa.a: "He's just on leave."

qa.q: How might Uma's little brother experience her shouting?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and confused, not knowing that her snapping came from worry about Papa.

passage: In their Pune flat, Aai had been home every day for three weeks now. Gautam knew the office had let her go; he'd heard it through the wall. He didn't ask anything.
